title: Streams
intro: Streams drain the land and shape it. These notes follow water from the first sheet of runoff to a channel and its drainage network, explain discharge, erosion and the sediment a stream carries, then walk down the longitudinal profile past waterfalls, fans, braided channels and meanders to the delta, and finish with floods and how people live with them.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how stream runoff fits into the hydrologic cycle and where streamflow comes from.
Describe how sheetwash, rills and headward erosion build channels and drainage networks.
Identify dendritic, radial, rectangular, trellis and parallel drainage and the geology each reflects.
Define drainage basins, divides and continental divides, and distinguish permanent from ephemeral streams.
Calculate discharge from cross-sectional area and velocity, and describe how velocity varies in a channel.
Compare bed, suspended and dissolved load, and explain competence, capacity and sorting by velocity.
Describe the longitudinal profile and explain how base level controls erosion and deposition.
Explain how canyons, terraces, waterfalls, alluvial fans, braided streams, meanders, oxbow lakes and deltas form.
Explain stream piracy, rejuvenation, and superposed, antecedent and diverted streams.
Compare seasonal and flash floods, their causes, and how recurrence intervals and flood control are used to manage flood risk.

sections.title: Streams drain the land

img.alt: A wide waterfall pouring over a rock ledge into a misty river gorge.

steps.title: Streams and stream runoff
bullets: **Streams** are channels of water that drain the landscape.
**Stream runoff** is water in motion over the land surface.
People use streamflow for drinking water, transportation, waste disposal, recreation, commerce, irrigation and energy generation.

img.alt: A pile of broken logs and branches left by a brown, swollen river, and an old drawing of people swept away by a flood.

steps.title: Runoff also causes problems
bullets: Stream runoff also causes many problems.
**Flooding** destroys lives and property.

img.alt: Aerial view of dry hills cut into a dense, branching pattern of valleys by running water.

steps.title: A geologic agent
bullets: Flowing water **erodes**, **transports** and **deposits** sediment, and it sculpts whole landscapes.
Earth is the only planet in the Solar System with flowing water. Without flowing water, Earth might look like Mars.

img.alt: A block diagram following a river from glaciers and steep mountain valleys, past waterfalls, rapids and braided channels, to wide meanders, oxbow lakes, natural levees and a delta at the sea.

steps.title: Part of the hydrologic cycle
bullets: Stream runoff is one part of the **hydrologic cycle**, the cycle of water leaving the sea and returning to it.
The other parts are **evaporation**, **transpiration** (water released by plants), **precipitation**, **infiltration** (water soaking into the ground) and **runoff**.
The picture follows a river from its mountain source to the sea. Each feature on it has its own topic in these notes.

img.alt: Block diagram of a valley with snow, a puddle, a swamp, a tributary joining a trunk stream, evaporation from the water and a water table below the ground feeding the stream.

steps.title: Where streamflow comes from
bullets: Streamflow begins as water is added to the surface. Water reaches a channel from **rain**, **snowmelt** and **groundwater discharge** (groundwater seeping into the channel).
Some streamflow is stored for a while in **lakes and wetlands**. Some soaks in (infiltrates) and becomes **groundwater**.

boxes.text: The Sun lifts water by evaporation, and gravity pulls it back downhill. Streams are the downhill part of that loop.
Three ways water gets into a stream: rain, melt, seep (groundwater).
Slide 81 review question: the hydrologic cycle is the cycle of water leaving and returning to the sea, not just clouds forming rain and not only groundwater flow.

sections.title: How a stream channel forms

img.alt: Aerial photo of a canyon landscape where thin sheets of water have carved many small channels on the slopes.

steps.title: Sheetwash
bullets: Streamflow begins as **sheetwash**: a thin surface layer of water that moves down the steepest slope.
Sheetwash erodes the ground and cuts tiny **rill** channels.
The rills join (coalesce), deepen and cut down, until the flow is concentrated in a **single channel**.

img.alt: Aerial photo of gullies eating back into a flat plain, with an arrow pointing to the head of a channel, and a 1 km scale bar.

steps.title: Headward erosion
bullets: **Headward erosion** is intense scouring where sheetflow pours into the uppermost end of a channel.
It makes the channel grow longer uphill. Headward erosion is how channels, and the drainage networks they belong to, expand to consume the landscape.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a winding trunk stream with smaller tributary channels joining it, each labelled with an arrow.

steps.title: Tributaries and trunk streams
bullets: Smaller **tributaries** join a larger **trunk stream**.
The whole set of linked channels is a **drainage network**. Drainage networks change over time.

boxes.text: Water scours hardest where it first drops into a channel, so the channel's upper end keeps eating back into the land.
Sheet → rills → one channel → network. Each stage gathers more water into fewer, deeper paths.
Headward erosion lengthens a channel UPSTREAM (toward its source), not downstream.

sourceNotes: Slides 8-10; slide 8 is the 4th edition Fig. 14.3.

sections.title: Drainage patterns

img.alt: Aerial photo of branching stream channels and an inset block diagram labelled Dendritic, with channels branching like a tree.

steps.title: Dendritic
bullets: Drainage networks often form geometric patterns that reflect the geology underneath.
**Dendritic** drainage branches like a tree. It forms where the rock being eroded is fairly **uniform (homogeneous)**.

img.alt: Block diagram of streams running outward in all directions from a volcano, labelled Radial, and a photo of a rounded hill.

steps.title: Radial
bullets: **Radial** drainage runs outward in all directions from a point uplift, such as a mesa or a volcano.

img.alt: Block diagram labelled Rectangular with channels turning at right angles along joints, and an aerial photo of straight valleys.

steps.title: Rectangular
bullets: **Rectangular** drainage follows **joints** in the bedrock that cross at 90° angles, so channels turn sharp corners.

img.alt: Aerial photo of long parallel ridges with a trunk stream and short tributaries, and an inset block diagram labelled Trellis showing resistant ridges.

steps.title: Trellis
bullets: **Trellis** drainage forms in **deformed (folded) layers** where resistant and weak rocks alternate.
Long streams run along the weak layers between resistant ridges, and short tributaries join them at right angles.

img.alt: Aerial photo of many streams running side by side down a slope, and an inset block diagram labelled Parallel.

steps.title: Parallel
bullets: **Parallel** drainage forms on a surface with a **uniform slope**, so the streams run side by side.

boxes.text: Water follows the easiest path. Weak layers, joints, a central peak or an even slope each set that path, so the pattern reveals the rock below.
Dendritic = tree. Radial = spokes from a volcano. Rectangular = right-angle joints. Trellis = garden trellis on folded layers. Parallel = one even slope.
Trellis and rectangular both have right-angle junctions. Trellis comes from alternating resistant and weak folded layers; rectangular comes from joints in the bedrock.

sections.title: Drainage basins and divides

img.alt: Aerial photo of grassy ridges and a block diagram showing the drainage basins of stream A and stream B separated by a drainage divide.

steps.title: Drainage basins and divides
bullets: A **drainage basin** (also called a **catchment** or **watershed**) is the land area that drains into one particular trunk stream.
A **drainage divide** separates neighbouring basins. A raindrop flows to one basin or the other depending on which side of the divide it lands.

img.alt: Map of North America coloured by where rivers drain: the Pacific, the Arctic Ocean, Hudson Bay, the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico, with the continental divide, the Mississippi basin and the Great Basin labelled.

steps.title: Scales and continental divides
bullets: Watersheds exist at every scale. Tiny tributaries have tiny watersheds; large continental rivers have huge ones.
A **continental divide** separates flow to different oceans. In North America, water on one side reaches the Pacific and on the other the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico, Hudson Bay or the Arctic Ocean.
On the map, the **Great Basin** has arrows pointing inward: its water does not reach any ocean.

img.alt: World map coloured by the ocean each region drains to, with dark grey endorheic basins in central Asia, Africa, Australia and western North America.

steps.title: Endorheic basins
bullets: An **endorheic basin** drains inward and never reaches the ocean.
The world map colours each region by the ocean it drains to. The dark grey regions are endorheic basins.

boxes.text: A divide is simply the high line between two slopes. Rain falling on each side runs downhill a different way.
Basin = bowl that collects the water. Divide = the rim between two bowls.
Catchment, watershed and drainage basin all mean the same thing in these notes.

sections.title: Permanent streams, discharge and flow

img.alt: Two block diagrams: a forested valley where a high water table feeds a flowing river, and a dry desert valley with cactus where the water table sits below the dry channel.

steps.title: Permanent and ephemeral streams
bullets: **Permanent streams** flow all year. They are common where there is abundant rainfall, groundwater discharge and little evaporation. The water table is high enough to feed the channel.
**Ephemeral streams** do not flow all year. They are common where annual rainfall is low, the water table is low and evaporation is high.

img.alt: A student wading in a stream with a measuring rod, and an inset drawing of a stream-gauging station with a current meter, the channel's cross-sectional area and a well that measures water depth.

steps.title: Discharge
bullets: **Discharge** is the volume of water passing a point in a channel per unit of time.
It is found by measuring the **cross-sectional area** of the channel and multiplying by the **flow velocity**.
Discharge changes with the seasons as precipitation and runoff change.

img.alt: A trapezoid-shaped channel cross-section labelled width, depth and area A, a red arrow for velocity v, the formula Q = A × v, and an example: 10 m wide times 2 m deep is 20 square metres, times 1.5 m/s gives 30 cubic metres per second.

steps.title: Working out discharge
bullets: **Discharge (Q) = cross-sectional area (A) × velocity (v)**.
For a simple channel, area ≈ width × depth. A channel 10 m wide and 2 m deep has an area of 20 m². If the water moves at 1.5 m/s, the discharge is 20 × 1.5 = **30 m³/s** (cubic metres per second).

img.alt: Photo of a curving stream with the far, outside bank steep and the inside bank low and sandy.

steps.title: Velocity across a channel
bullets: Velocity is not the same everywhere in a channel. **Friction** slows the water along the edges; water flows **fastest in the deeper centre**.
In a curved channel, the fastest water swings to the **outside of the curve**, which is scoured and deepened.

img.alt: Block diagram of a stream bed with arrows showing laminar flow, turbulent flow around boulders, an eddy, a whirlpool, and water rotating as it slows along the bank.

steps.title: Turbulent flow
bullets: Streamflow is **turbulent**: chaotic and erratic, with lots of mixing by **eddies** (swirls).
Eddies scour sediment and bedrock.

boxes.text: Water drags against the bed and banks, so it moves slowest there and fastest in the deep middle, away from the friction.
Q = A × v. More area or faster water, more discharge.
Discharge is a VOLUME per time (for example m³/s), not a speed. Velocity alone is in m/s.

sourceNotes: Slides 19-22; Fig. 14.6a, b and 14.7a, b.
Area ≈ width × depth and the worked numbers in the discharge diagram are an illustration, not slide values.

sections.title: How streams erode

img.alt: Photo of brown, churning floodwater pouring over a weir around a half-submerged tree.

steps.title: Where the energy comes from
bullets: Streamflow does work by turning **potential energy** (water high up) into **kinetic energy** (moving water).
That energy comes from **gravity** acting on water that the **Sun** lifted up by evaporation.

img.alt: Photo of a rocky stream bed covered with broken, flat slabs of rock beside a wooded bank.

steps.title: Four ways streams erode
bullets: Streams **scour** (sweep away loose material), **break** rock, **abrade** (grind it with the sediment they carry) and **dissolve** material.

img.alt: Photos of a narrow, smooth-walled slot canyon and of round holes drilled through pale bedrock, one big enough for a person to stand in.

steps.title: Potholes
bullets: **Potholes** form where turbulent eddies swirl sand and gravel round and round.
This abrasive material drills holes into the bedrock.

boxes.text: Moving water carries grit. Swirling grit acts like sandpaper or a drill on the rock it touches.
Scour, break, abrade, dissolve: SBAD.
Potholes are drilled by the sand and gravel the eddies swirl, not by clear water alone.

sourceNotes: Slides 23-25; Fig. 14.8a.

sections.title: Sediment load, competence and capacity

img.alt: Cut-away drawing of a stream bed: boulders rolling, pebbles hopping (saltation), a magnified circle of dissolved ions and another of tiny suspended clay flakes.

steps.title: Three kinds of load
bullets: The material a stream moves is its **sediment load**.
**Bed load**: the larger grains that roll, slip and bounce along the bed. The bouncing movement is called **saltation**.
**Suspended load**: fine particles (silt and clay) carried within the flow.
**Dissolved load**: ions released by the weathering of minerals.

img.alt: Animation of a stream from the side: a boulder rolls along the bed, a pebble bounces in hops, small specks of silt and clay drift in the water, and plus and minus ions move evenly through it.

steps.title: Watch the loads move
bullets: Boulders and pebbles stay on or near the bed. Silt and clay ride inside the water. Ions are dissolved and cannot be seen.

img.alt: Photo of a mountain stream with whitewater rushing between large rounded boulders.

steps.title: Competence and capacity
bullets: **Competence** is the **largest grain size** a stream can move.
**Capacity** is the **total load** (coarse, fine and dissolved) a stream can carry.
Transport changes with discharge. At high discharge, cobbles and boulders that sit stranded at low discharge can move.

img.alt: Photo of a stream bank where gravel lies near the channel and finer sand and mud spread across the flatter, quieter area.

steps.title: Deposition sorts the grains
bullets: **Competence drops as velocity drops**, so grains fall out as the water slows.
The water **sorts** them by size.

img.alt: Three boxes under a bar going from fast to slow: the channel with large grey gravel, point bars and levees with sand, and slack water with very fine mud of silt and clay.

steps.title: Where each size settles
bullets: **Gravel** settles where the water is fastest, in the **channel**.
**Sand** settles where it is a little slower: **point bars** and **levees**.
**Mud** (silt and clay) settles in **slack (still) water**.

boxes.text: A fast stream has the energy to move big grains. As it slows, it drops the heaviest grains first, so each place ends up with one size.
Competence = the biggest piece. Capacity = the whole truckload.
Saltation is part of the BED load (grains bouncing along the bed), not the suspended load. Silt and clay are suspended; ions are dissolved.

sections.title: The longitudinal profile

img.alt: Block diagram of a stream from its headwaters through a trunk stream, meanders and floodplain to a delta at standing water, with cross-sections A, B and C getting wider and flatter downstream.

steps.title: A concave-up curve
bullets: A stream's character changes with distance downstream.
Cross-section A near the source is a narrow V; cross-section C near the mouth is wide and flat.

img.alt: Graph of elevation against distance from the mouth: a curve that drops steeply from the source and flattens toward the mouth, ending at base level.

steps.title: From source to mouth
bullets: The **longitudinal profile** is the stream's elevation plotted along its length. On average it is a **concave-up curve**: steep near the source, flattening toward the mouth.
Flow and sediment transport change along this profile.

img.alt: Photo of a mountain river rushing white over boulders between forested banks.

steps.title: Near the headwaters
bullets: Near the source, the **gradient is steep**, **discharge is low**, sediment is **coarse** and the channel is **straight and rocky**.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a broad river winding across farmland, with old curved channel scars beside it.

steps.title: Toward the mouth
bullets: Toward the mouth, the **gradient flattens**, **discharge increases**, grains are **smaller** and the channel develops broad **meander belts**.

img.alt: A comparison table: near the headwaters the gradient is steep, discharge low, sediment coarse and the channel straight and rocky; toward the mouth the gradient flattens, discharge increases, grains are smaller and the channel has broad meander belts.

steps.title: Side by side
bullets: Discharge goes **up** downstream because tributaries keep adding water, even as the slope goes **down**.

boxes.text: Tributaries keep adding water downstream, so discharge rises while the slope eases. The stream no longer needs a steep slope to move its water.
Steep, small, coarse, straight at the top; flat, big, fine, wiggly at the bottom.
Discharge INCREASES toward the mouth even though the gradient decreases. Don't assume a gentler slope means less water.

sourceNotes: 'Tributaries keep adding water' is an explanation added for clarity.

sections.title: Base level

img.alt: Photo of a tall, thin waterfall dropping from a ledge of layered rock into a pool at the bottom of a steep gorge.

steps.title: What base level is
bullets: **Base level** is the lowest point to which a stream can erode.
The **ultimate base level** is **sea level**. A **lake** is a **local (temporary) base level**.
A ledge of **resistant rock** can also set a local base level. Erosion slowly removes the ledge and restores the smooth profile.

img.alt: A stream profile curving down to the sea with a dashed line for sea level as the ultimate base level, a lake and a resistant ledge as local base levels, and two boxes: raise base level for more deposition, lower base level for faster erosion.

steps.title: Raising or lowering base level
bullets: A change in base level makes the stream readjust.
**Raising** base level causes **more deposition**.
**Lowering** base level **speeds up erosion**.

img.alt: A graph sorting all of Earth's surface by elevation, from the peak of Mount Everest at 8,848 m down to the Mariana Trench at minus 10,911 m, with sea level marked across it.

steps.title: How high is the land?
bullets: This graph sorts Earth's whole surface by elevation, from the top of **Mount Everest (8,848 m)** to the bottom of the **Mariana Trench (−10,911 m)**.
Sea level, the ultimate base level, is the line that the land's streams erode toward.

boxes.text: Water cannot flow below the water body it drains into, so a stream cannot cut deeper than that level.
Raise the floor, the stream fills in. Drop the floor, the stream digs.
A lake or a waterfall ledge is only a LOCAL, temporary base level. The ultimate base level is sea level.

sourceNotes: Slides 30-31. Slide 31 is a Wikipedia elevation histogram with only a title.

steps.title: Stair-step canyons
bullets: Rock layers often alternate between **stronger** and **weaker** rocks.
Erosion of such layers makes a **stair-step profile**: stronger rocks form **vertical cliffs** and weaker rocks form **sloped walls**.

img.alt: Two block diagrams: at Time 1 a raised base level lets a valley fill with yellow alluvium; at Time 2 a lowered base level lets the stream cut down, leaving terraces on both sides.

steps.title: Valley fill and terraces
bullets: A **rise in base level** or a **drop in discharge** makes the valley **fill with alluvium** (stream sediment).
If base level **falls** or discharge **increases**, the stream **cuts down** into the alluvium and makes a new, lower floodplain.
**Paired terraces** are the leftover pieces of the old floodplain on both sides.

img.alt: Four block diagrams over time: swampy low-relief land is uplifted, becomes well-drained land cut by streams, then valleys broaden, and finally a new low-relief landscape forms.

steps.title: Landscapes wear down
bullets: Landscapes change over time, mostly because of streamflow.
When base level drops, streams cut into the old surface, valleys widen and hills erode. Eventually the land is worn down to the **new base level**.

img.alt: Photos of a broad waterfall tumbling over many rocky ledges and of a tall, single waterfall in a misty forest.

steps.title: Rapids and waterfalls
bullets: **Waterfalls** are places where a stream cascades or free-falls down a very steep gradient.
The falling water scours a **plunge pool** at the base. Erosion at the base undercuts the rock above until it collapses.
Waterfalls are **temporary base levels**.

img.alt: Aerial photo of Niagara Falls and a block diagram showing Lake Erie, the falls, Niagara Gorge, the Lockport Dolostone caprock, the Niagara Escarpment and Lake Ontario.

steps.title: Niagara Falls
bullets: Lake Erie drops **55 m** to Lake Ontario over Niagara Falls.
The **dolostone caprock** is resistant. The **shale** underneath erodes, and blocks of unsupported dolostone collapse.
So the falls keep moving **south (upstream) toward Lake Erie**. Erosion since the ice age glaciers melted has carved **Niagara Gorge**.

boxes.text: Hard rock resists and stands as a cliff or a falls lip; soft rock beneath wears away and leaves the hard rock unsupported.
Terraces are bathtub rings of an old, higher floodplain.
Niagara Falls retreats UPSTREAM (south toward Lake Erie), not downstream toward Lake Ontario.

sections.title: Alluvial fans and braided streams

img.alt: Aerial photo of a fan of sediment spreading out from the mouth of a canyon at the foot of a mountain front.

steps.title: Alluvial fans
bullets: **Alluvial fans** are cone-shaped, fan-shaped deposits that build at the **base of a mountain front**.
Sediment drops out quickly where the stream's **gradient suddenly decreases**.
The **coarsest** material is near the mouth of the canyon; sediment becomes **finer and thinner** with distance.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a wide grey valley floor crossed by many shallow channels splitting and rejoining around gravel bars.

steps.title: Braided streams
bullets: **Braided streams** form where channels are **choked with sediment**.
Flow is forced around the sediment, and the splitting and rejoining flow builds **sand and gravel bars**.
The bars are unstable: they form and erode quickly, and water spreads across **many channels** in the valley.

boxes.text: When a stream suddenly slows or has more sediment than it can carry, it drops the extra load and builds fans and bars.
Braided = many strands woven together, like braided hair.
Braided streams have MANY shallow channels around bars. Meandering streams have ONE looping channel.

sourceNotes: Slides 38-39; Fig. 14.15a, b.

images.alt: Aerial photo of a fan of sediment spreading out from the mouth of a canyon at the foot of a mountain front.

sections.title: Meandering streams and oxbow lakes

img.alt: Satellite image of a river looping across a forested plain, with a meander, an oxbow lake, an abandoned meander, point bars and a meander neck labelled, and a 20 km scale bar.

steps.title: Meanders
bullets: On the gentle, low-gradient part of the profile, channels form tightly looping bends called **meanders**.

img.alt: Four map drawings over time: a gently curving stream erodes on the outside of bends and deposits on the inside, grows point bars, forms a narrow meander neck and finally cuts off, leaving an oxbow lake.

steps.title: Cut bank and point bar
bullets: The fastest water erodes the **outside** of a bend, called the **cut bank**.
The **inside** of the bend, the **point bar**, is where sediment is deposited.
Over time meanders grow more **sinuous** (loopy) by cut-bank erosion and point-bar growth, until they are eventually cut off.

img.alt: Two photos of the same river: a steep, crumbling earth bank on the outside of a bend, and a low, pale gravel point bar on the inside of a bend.

steps.title: In a real stream
bullets: Fast flow scours the base of the cut bank, which collapses into the channel. The flow carries the fallen material away.
Slower water inside the bend drops sediment, and the point bar grows toward the channel.

img.alt: Aerial photo of curved lakes and old channels beside a winding river, above a satellite image of a looping river with oxbow lakes and abandoned meanders labelled.

steps.title: Cutoffs and oxbow lakes
bullets: A **meander cutoff** happens when two cut banks grow toward each other and the **meander neck** thins.
During a flood, fast water jumps out of the channel and erodes through the neck.
The cut-off loop becomes an **oxbow lake**, which slowly fills with sediment. Old oxbow lakes show up as curved scars on the floodplain.

img.alt: Animation in map view: a gentle bend in a blue river grows into a large loop, with the cut bank eroding on the outside and a sandy point bar growing inside; the neck thins, the river cuts through it, and the loop is left as an oxbow lake beside the new, shorter channel.

steps.title: Watch a meander grow
bullets: The loop grows outward at the cut bank while the point bar fills in behind it.
Once the river cuts through the neck, it takes the **shorter path** and abandons the loop.

boxes.text: In a bend, the fastest water is thrown to the outside and erodes it, while the slower water on the inside drops sediment. The bend migrates sideways.
Cut bank = cut away (erosion, outside). Point bar = pile up (deposition, inside).
Erosion is on the OUTSIDE of a bend (cut bank) and deposition on the INSIDE (point bar). Swapping them is a common mistake.

sourceNotes: Slides 41-44; Fig. 14.16a, b. Slide 46 is a video link on meandering river deposits.

images.alt: Satellite image of a river looping across a forested plain, with a meander, an oxbow lake, an abandoned meander, point bars and a meander neck labelled, and a 20 km scale bar.

Four map drawings over time: a gently curving stream erodes on the outside of bends and deposits on the inside, grows point bars, forms a narrow meander neck and finally cuts off, leaving an oxbow lake.
Two photos of the same river: a steep, crumbling earth bank on the outside of a bend, and a low, pale gravel point bar on the inside of a bend.
Aerial photo of curved lakes and old channels beside a winding river, above a satellite image of a looping river with oxbow lakes and abandoned meanders labelled.

Animation in map view: a gentle bend in a blue river grows into a large loop, with the cut bank eroding on the outside and a sandy point bar growing inside; the neck thins, the river cuts through it, and the loop is left as an oxbow lake beside the new, shorter channel.

img.alt: Two block diagrams: first a stream's headward erosion eats into the divide next to the Persephone River; then it has captured that river, leaving a dry channel and a water gap.

steps.title: Stream piracy
bullets: **Stream piracy** is when one stream **captures** another stream's flow.
A stream with vigorous **headward erosion** cuts through the divide between two watersheds and steals the neighbouring stream's water.
Downstream of the point of capture, the old channel **dries up**.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a river winding in deep, tight loops cut far down into layered rock.

steps.title: Stream rejuvenation
bullets: **Stream rejuvenation** starts when **base level falls**.
Meanders that formed on a gentle slope cut straight down when **uplift** raises the land, like a chainsaw. This makes **incised meanders**.

img.alt: Two block diagrams: a stream flows on flat young layers above folded older rock and an unconformity; later it has cut down through the folded rock, keeping its old path and leaving a water gap.

steps.title: Superposed streams
bullets: **Superposed streams** cross deformed rock but ignore its structure.
They first formed on **younger, flat-lying layers**. As the stream cut down into the **older, deformed rock** below, it kept the path it had before.

img.alt: Block diagrams of drainage before uplift, then a rising mountain range that a stream either cuts straight through (antecedent) or is pushed around onto a new course (diverted).

steps.title: Antecedent and diverted streams
bullets: If a mountain range rises across a stream's path, the stream either cuts across it or is diverted.
If **erosion is faster than uplift**, the stream cuts through the range: an **antecedent stream**.
If **uplift is faster than erosion**, the range deflects the stream: a **diverted stream**.

boxes.text: A stream keeps working on whatever surface it already has. Whether it keeps its course depends on whether it can cut down as fast as the land changes.
Antecedent = 'ante' (before): the stream was there before the mountains and won the race.
A superposed stream was set on younger flat layers ABOVE the structure; an antecedent stream was there BEFORE the uplift. Both cut across structure, for different reasons.

sections.title: Deltas

img.alt: Three maps of deltas: a triangular delta on the Atlantic coast of Africa, an arc-shaped delta on the Mediterranean, and a bird's-foot delta in the Gulf of Mexico.

steps.title: What a delta is
bullets: **Deltas** are sediment deposited at the **mouth** of a stream. Where a stream enters standing water, the current slows, loses competence and drops its sediment.
On top of a delta the stream splits into a fan of **distributary channels**. They form because sediment dropped in the channel diverts the flow.
A delta's shape (**Δ-shaped**, **arc-like** or **bird's-foot**) depends on sediment supply and on the strength of the river compared with the ocean currents and waves that carry sediment away.

img.alt: Satellite image of a delta lobe with channels branching into the sea and narrow strips of green natural levees along them.

steps.title: Abandoned lobes
bullets: Abandoned **delta lobes** no longer get sediment from distributary channels.
They **compact and sink (subside)**, and storm waves attack the delta front.

img.alt: Map of the Mississippi delta showing six old delta lobes, A to F, built at different times over the last 7,500 years, around New Orleans and Baton Rouge.

steps.title: Avulsion
bullets: The main channel feeding a delta can **jump** to a new location to find a steeper, shorter path to the sea. This is **avulsion**.
The Mississippi River has done this several times in the past **7,500 years**. Each old lobe (A to F on the map) is a past position of the delta.

img.alt: Map of eastern China with coloured lines showing where the lower Huang (Yellow) River flowed in different periods from 2300 BCE to today, some reaching the sea north and some south of the Shandong Peninsula.

steps.title: The Huang (Yellow) River
bullets: The lower Huang (Yellow) River has changed course many times since 2300 BCE.
Its mouth has moved to both sides of the **Shandong Peninsula**, hundreds of kilometres apart.

boxes.text: When river water meets still water it slows abruptly, so it can no longer carry its load and the sediment piles up.
Distributaries are the reverse of tributaries: they split water off instead of adding it.
Slide 80 review question: deltas are sedimentary accumulations at BASE LEVEL (where the stream meets standing water), not at point bars or river avulsions.

sourceNotes: Slides 51-55; Fig. 14.17, 14.17c, 14.18; slides 54-55 are two versions of a Huang and Yangtze map.
Slide 80 is a review question (answer C, base level).

sections.title: Floods

img.alt: A helicopter lifting a person from churning floodwater, and an aerial photo of a town and highway surrounded by flood water.

steps.title: Raging waters
bullets: During a **flood**, discharge and velocity increase and water spills out of the channel, covering the land next to it.
Flood water scours floodplains, changes the landscape and destroys buildings.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a village with houses standing in brown flood water and people wading between them.

steps.title: Seasonal floods
bullets: **Seasonal floods** build over hours or days, so people have time to evacuate. But so many people live on floodplains and delta plains that losses are still huge.

Seasonal floods come back every year. **Monsoons**, the tropical rains of the Indian subcontinent, bring long periods of rain and severe flooding. In **1990** the monsoon killed **100,000** people in Bangladesh.

img.alt: Two satellite images of where the Illinois, Mississippi and Missouri Rivers meet: thin rivers in August 1991, and wide dark flood water covering the land in August 1993.

steps.title: Mississippi and Missouri Rivers, 1993
bullets: In spring 1993 the **jet stream** sat over the midwestern U.S. and trapped moist air from the Gulf of Mexico, so rain fell for a long time.
From July 1993 the flood lasted **79 days** and covered **40,000 square miles**. 50 people died, 55,000 homes were destroyed and damage reached **$12 billion**.

img.alt: Map of Pakistan with a wide blue band of flooded land along the Indus River from the north to Karachi, and a photo of submerged fields.

steps.title: Indus Valley, Pakistan, 2010
bullets: In 2010 a huge band of land along the **Indus River** in Pakistan was flooded.

img.alt: Two satellite images of the same part of Pakistan on August 27, 2021 and August 27, 2022; in 2022 a large dark blue area of flood water covers land that was dry the year before.

steps.title: Indus Valley, 2021 and 2022
bullets: Satellite images of the same day in 2021 and 2022 show how much of the Indus valley flooded in 2022.

img.alt: An old drawing of people and houses swept away in a flood, and a photo of a helicopter rescuing a person from rushing floodwater.

steps.title: Flash floods
bullets: **Flash floods** rise so quickly that escape may be impossible: a fast-moving wall of water full of debris.
They come from unusually **intense rainfall**, a **dam collapse** or a **levee failure**, with little warning.
In **1889** a flash flood from a dam failure killed **2,300** people in Johnstown, Pennsylvania.

img.alt: Photo of a house knocked off its foundation and a wrecked bridge in a rocky river valley after a flood.

steps.title: Big Thompson River, Colorado, 1976
bullets: On July 31, 1976, **19 cm** of rain fell on the Rockies in about an hour.
Discharge in the Big Thompson River rose to **four times** the largest ever recorded. Rock and soil joined the flow, houses, bridges and roads vanished, and **144** people died.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a Calgary neighbourhood almost completely surrounded by the brown, flooded Bow River in 2013.

steps.title: Calgary, 2013
bullets: In June 2013 the **Bow River** flooded neighbourhoods in Calgary.

img.alt: Four panels: abrupt heavy rain dumping water quickly; long continuous rain that has already filled the soil's pores; sudden warm weather melting snow; and a natural or artificial dam breaking.

steps.title: What causes floods
bullets: Floods happen when **abrupt, heavy rain** dumps a lot of water quickly,
when **long, continuous rain** has already **saturated** the soil,
when **abrupt warm weather** melts winter snow fast,
or when a **natural or artificial dam** breaks.

boxes.text: Once soil is full of water or frozen, rain and melt can't soak in, so almost all of it runs straight to the channels.
Seasonal = slow and yearly (time to leave). Flash = sudden wall of water (no time).
Seasonal floods allow time to evacuate, yet they still cause enormous losses because so many people live on floodplains.

sourceNotes: Slides 58-65 and 45 (Bow River, Calgary, 2013 photo); Fig. 14.1, 14.23a-c, 14.24a, b. Slides 61-62 are the Indus 2010 map and 2021/2022 satellite images.
Slide 65 repeats the Big Thompson photo, so the causes list uses an original diagram.

sections.title: Living with floods

img.alt: Photo of water rushing through a broken levee, and a drawing of an artificial levee holding back river water above the old ground surface, with water seeping under it, a slump and puddles on the dry side.

steps.title: Levees and dams
bullets: **Flood control** is expensive and sometimes useless. **Dams** hold water back from trunk streams.
**Artificial levees** and flood walls make the channel hold more water, but they pass **stronger flooding downstream**.
Levees are sometimes **overtopped** or **undermined**.

img.alt: Map of the Mississippi River at Davenport and Rock Island with the areas a 100-year (1%) flood would cover in light blue and a 500-year (0.2%) flood in green.

steps.title: Floodways
bullets: People living on floodplains face hard choices: move, or eventually suffer a catastrophic loss.
Defining **floodways** (places designed to carry floods) and moving people and buildings out of them can reduce the losses.
After the 1972 flood in Rapid City, South Dakota (238 deaths), houses and motels were raised or moved and most of the floodplain became parks.

img.alt: Graph of discharge in cubic feet per second against recurrence interval in years on a logarithmic scale; the points fall on a rising straight line from about 1 year to over 100 years.

steps.title: Recurrence intervals
bullets: Flood risk is calculated as a **probability**.
Plotting discharges against their **recurrence interval** on semi-logarithmic paper gives a **straight line**. The chance of a given discharge can be read from the graph.

img.alt: Bars showing that a 2-year flood has a 50% chance each year, a 100-year flood a 1% chance and a 500-year flood a 0.2% chance.

steps.title: The chance each year
bullets: A **2-year flood** has a **50%** chance of happening in any year; a **100-year flood** a **1%** chance; a **500-year flood** a **0.2%** chance.
A '100-year flood' can happen two years in a row; it just has a 1% chance each year.

img.alt: Block diagram of a valley with a non-flood channel and dashed lines marking the limit of the 2-year flood (50% probability) close to the stream and the 100-year flood (1% probability) farther out.

steps.title: Flood risk maps
bullets: Hydrologic data are used to draw **flood risk maps**, so regulators can manage risk. Building in flood-prone places is tightly regulated.
Flood risk is carried by homeowners, insurance companies, lenders and government agencies.

img.alt: Map of central Calgary where the Bow and Elbow Rivers meet, showing the normal water surface, the floodway of deep, fast water and the floodplain of shallow, slow water in 2013.

steps.title: Calgary's floodway and floodplain
bullets: This map of central Calgary in 2013 separates the **floodway** (deep, fast-moving water) from the **floodplain** (shallow, slow-moving water).

img.alt: Graph of Red River discharge in cubic metres per second against return period in years on logarithmic scales, with big floods labelled 1776, 1826, 1852, 1997 and others near the top right.

steps.title: Red River flood frequency
bullets: The same kind of graph for the **Red River** marks its largest floods, such as 1826, 1852 and 1997, at the long-recurrence end.

img.alt: Radar satellite image from May 1, 1997 showing a huge blue area of flood water south of Winnipeg along the Red River, the floodway around the city and the Brunkild dike extension.

steps.title: Red River, 1997
bullets: In **May 1997** the Red River flooded a huge area south of Winnipeg. The Floodway carried water around the city.

img.alt: Radar map of the Red River flood extent on May 2, 2011, from the U.S. into Manitoba, with flooded areas in blue.

steps.title: Red River, 2011
bullets: The Red River flooded again in **2011**, shown here by radar satellite imagery.

img.alt: Map of Winnipeg showing the Red River Floodway channel curving around the east side of the city, its inlet and outlet control structures, and the West Dike.

steps.title: The Red River Floodway
bullets: Winnipeg's **Floodway** is a channel that takes Red River flood water **around the city**, with control structures at its inlet and outlet and dikes to the west.

boxes.text: Levees squeeze the water into a narrower space, so it rises higher and moves the flood problem downstream.
% chance each year = 100 ÷ recurrence interval. 100-year → 1%, 2-year → 50%.
A 100-year flood is not one that happens only once a century. It has a 1% chance EVERY year.

img.alt: A river channel under cleanup with steel walls and a crane, a pipe draining into a stream, and a rainbow sheen of oil on water.

steps.title: Pollution
bullets: Rivers have guided where people settle for hundreds of thousands of years. They provide drinking water, food, transport, energy, recreation and waste disposal.
Rivers are still abused. Pollution includes human and animal **sewage**, **heavy metals**, **fertilizers**, **pesticides**, **road salt**, **oil** and **toxic wastes**.
The Housatonic River in Massachusetts is being cleaned of sediment contaminated with **PCBs**.

img.alt: A tall concrete dam under an arch bridge, an aerial view of fields dotted with shining farm ponds, and a reservoir's branching arms.

steps.title: Dams
bullets: People have dammed rivers widely, with **both good and bad** results.
The bright dots in the aerial photo are sunlight reflecting off dammed farm ponds in central Missouri.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a long concrete canal carrying water across a desert past houses and roads.

steps.title: Too much taken
bullets: In many places, especially **dry (arid)** ones, people take so much river water for **irrigation and industry** that too little is left for the river's natural water and ecological functions.

boxes.text: Whatever goes into the watershed (salt, fertilizer, oil) ends up in the river that drains it.
Rivers give: water, food, transport, energy, fun, waste disposal. People take too much and put in too much.
Dams have BOTH positive and negative consequences; the deck does not call them only harmful.

table.title: Stream features at a glance
head: Feature
Where it forms
What makes it
rows: Sand and gravel swirled by turbulent eddies

Sudden drop in gradient makes the stream drop its load
Flow splits around unstable sand and gravel bars
A flood cuts through a meander neck
The stream cuts down into its old floodplain
Mouth of a stream at standing water
Current slows, loses competence and drops sediment

cards.back: Water in motion over the land surface. It is one part of the hydrologic cycle.
The cycle of water leaving the sea and returning to it: evaporation, transpiration, precipitation, infiltration and runoff.
cards.short: Water leaves the sea and comes back

cards.back: Water released into the air by plants. One part of the hydrologic cycle.
Water soaking into the ground, where some of it becomes groundwater.
A thin surface layer of water that moves down the steepest slope. It is where streamflow begins.
cards.short: Thin sheet of water down the slope

cards.back: A tiny channel cut by sheetwash. Rills join, deepen and cut down into one channel.
Intense scouring where sheetflow enters the top of a channel. It lengthens the channel uphill and lets networks expand.
cards.short: Channel grows uphill at its head

cards.back: A smaller stream that joins a larger trunk stream.
cards.short: Small stream joining a bigger one

cards.back: The whole set of linked channels: tributaries feeding a trunk stream.
A drainage pattern branching like a tree. It forms on fairly uniform rock.
Streams running outward in all directions from a point uplift such as a volcano or mesa.
Channels that follow joints crossing at 90° in the bedrock.
A pattern in folded layers of alternating resistant and weak rock: long streams in weak layers, short tributaries at right angles.
Streams running side by side down a surface with a uniform slope.
cards.short: Side by side on an even slope

cards.back: The land area that drains into one trunk stream. Also called a catchment or watershed.
The high line separating neighbouring drainage basins. A raindrop goes to one basin or the other depending on its side.
A divide that separates flow to different oceans.
A stream that flows all year. Common with abundant rain, groundwater discharge and low evaporation.
A stream that does not flow all year. Common with low rainfall, a low water table and high evaporation.
The volume of water passing a point per unit of time: cross-sectional area × flow velocity.
A swirl in turbulent flow. Eddies mix the water and scour sediment and bedrock.
A hole drilled into bedrock by sand and gravel swirled by turbulent eddies.
Larger grains that roll, slip and bounce (saltate) along the stream bed.
The bouncing movement of bed-load grains along a stream bed.
Fine particles (silt and clay) carried within the flow.
cards.short: Silt and clay in the water

cards.back: Ions from the weathering of minerals, carried dissolved in the water.
The largest grain size a stream can transport. It drops as velocity drops.
The maximum total load (coarse, fine and dissolved) a stream can carry.
A stream's elevation along its length: on average a concave-up curve, steep at the source and flat near the mouth.
The lowest point a stream can erode to. Ultimate base level is sea level; a lake is a local base level.
cards.short: Lowest level it can cut to

cards.back: A leftover piece of an old, higher floodplain, left when a stream cuts down into its alluvium.
cards.short: Step left from an old floodplain

cards.back: A pool scoured at the base of a waterfall by the falling water.
A fan-shaped deposit at the base of a mountain front where the stream gradient suddenly drops. Coarsest near the canyon mouth.
A stream choked with sediment, splitting into many channels around unstable sand and gravel bars.
The outside of a meander bend, where the fastest water erodes the bank.
The inside of a meander bend, where slower water deposits sediment.
A curved lake left when a meander is cut off at its neck during a flood.
When a stream with vigorous headward erosion cuts through a divide and captures another stream's flow.
A stream that keeps cutting through a rising mountain range because erosion outpaces uplift.
When the main channel feeding a delta jumps to a new, steeper and shorter path to the sea.

quiz.q: Which list gives the three ways water is added to a stream channel?
quiz.why: Rain, snowmelt and groundwater discharge add water to a channel. Evaporation and infiltration remove water from the stream.

quiz.q: What is the hydrologic cycle?
options: Water leaving the sea and returning to it
Water entering and leaving the human body
The yearly rise and fall of a river
quiz.why: The hydrologic cycle is the whole loop of water leaving the sea (evaporation) and coming back to it (runoff and groundwater).

quiz.q: How do stream channels and drainage networks grow uphill into the landscape?
options: By deposition on point bars inside each bend
By avulsion of the channel at the mouth
By headward erosion at the top of the channel
By saltation of pebbles along the bed
By a rise in base level that fills the valley
quiz.why: Headward erosion is intense scouring where sheetflow enters the uppermost part of a channel, so the channel lengthens upslope.

quiz.q: Streams flow outward in every direction from the top of a volcano. Which drainage pattern is this?
quiz.why: Radial drainage develops from a point uplift such as a volcano or mesa.

img.alt: Block diagram of streams running outward in all directions from a volcano, labelled Radial, and a photo of a rounded hill.

quiz.q: A drainage pattern branches like a tree. What does this tell you about the rock below?
options: It is folded into hard and soft layers
It has a single steep, even slope
It is a recently uplifted volcano
quiz.why: Dendritic drainage forms on material that is relatively homogeneous, so no particular direction is easier for the water.

quiz.q: Trellis drainage develops where...
options: the land slopes evenly in one direction
deformed layers of resistant and weak rock alternate
a single peak rises above flat land
the bedrock has joints crossing at right angles
the stream has reached its ultimate base level
quiz.why: Trellis drainage forms in deformed strata with alternating resistant and weak rocks.

img.alt: Aerial photo of long parallel ridges with a trunk stream and short tributaries, and an inset block diagram labelled Trellis showing resistant ridges.

quiz.q: What separates two neighbouring drainage basins?
quiz.why: A drainage divide is the high line between basins. A raindrop goes to one basin or the other depending on which side it lands.

quiz.q: Which conditions favour an ephemeral stream?
options: Abundant rain, high water table, low evaporation
A rise in base level and more discharge
A uniform slope and homogeneous rock
Low rainfall, low water table, high evaporation
quiz.why: Ephemeral streams do not flow all year and are common where rainfall is low, the water table is low and evaporation is high.

img.alt: Two block diagrams: a forested valley where a high water table feeds a flowing river, and a dry desert valley with cactus where the water table sits below the dry channel.

quiz.q: A channel is 8 m wide and 2 m deep, and the water moves at 3 m/s. What is the discharge?
quiz.why: Discharge = area × velocity = (8 × 2) × 3 = 16 × 3 = 48 m³/s.

quiz.q: Where in a straight channel does water flow fastest?
options: In the deeper centre, away from the edges
quiz.why: Friction slows the water along the edges, so water flows faster in the deeper centre.

quiz.q: In a curved channel, which part is scoured and deepened?
quiz.why: The maximum velocity is swept to the outside of the curve, which is preferentially scoured and deepened.

quiz.q: Where does the energy that lets streams do erosional work come from?
options: Gravity acting on water the Sun lifted up
Wind blowing across the water surface
quiz.why: Streams convert potential energy to kinetic energy. The energy comes from gravity acting on water that was raised by the Sun through evaporation.

quiz.q: How do potholes form in stream beds?
options: Dissolved ions eat holes in the bedrock
Ice wedges pry the rock apart
Groundwater collapses the rock from below
Sand and gravel swirled by eddies drill the rock
quiz.why: Potholes are formed by sand and gravel swirled by turbulent eddies; the abrasive material drills holes in the bedrock.

img.alt: Photos of a narrow, smooth-walled slot canyon and of round holes drilled through pale bedrock, one big enough for a person to stand in.

quiz.q: Pebbles bounce along a stream bed in short hops. What is this movement called, and which load is it part of?
quiz.why: Bed load grains roll, slip and bounce along the bed. The bouncing is saltation.

img.alt: Cut-away drawing of a stream bed: boulders rolling, pebbles hopping (saltation), a magnified circle of dissolved ions and another of tiny suspended clay flakes.

quiz.q: Silt and clay carried within the flow make up the...
quiz.why: Suspended load is fine particles (silt and clay) entrained in the flow.

quiz.q: What is a stream's competence?
options: The total amount of sediment it can carry
The volume of water passing per second
The lowest level it can erode to
The largest grain size it can move
The number of tributaries it has
quiz.why: Competence is the maximum grain size transported. Capacity is the maximum total load.

quiz.q: As a stream slows, which sediment settles in slack water?
quiz.why: Competence decreases with velocity. Gravel settles in fast channels, sand on point bars and levees, and mud in slack water.

quiz.q: Compared with the headwaters, a stream near its mouth has...
options: a flatter gradient, more discharge and finer grains
lower discharge and a straighter, rockier channel
a steeper gradient and coarser, rockier sediment
the same gradient but much less water in it
a rocky channel lined with coarse gravel
quiz.why: Near the mouth the gradient flattens, discharge increases, grains are smaller and broad meander belts develop.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate base level for most streams?
quiz.why: Base level is the lowest point to which a stream can erode. The ultimate base level is sea level; lakes and ledges are local base levels.

quiz.q: A dam raises the base level of a stream. What happens upstream of it?
options: The stream becomes braided at once
quiz.why: Raising base level results in an increase in deposition; lowering base level accelerates erosion.

quiz.q: A canyon wall has steep cliffs separated by gentler slopes. What explains this stair-step shape?
options: The stream changed direction many times
Rising base level filling the valley
Alternating stronger and weaker rock layers
quiz.why: Stronger rocks produce vertical cliffs and weaker rocks produce sloped walls, giving a stair-step profile.

img.alt: Photo of the Grand Canyon's stepped walls, and a drawing of hard and soft layers eroding over time into a stair-step canyon.

quiz.q: Paired terraces on both sides of a valley are...
options: remnants of an older, higher floodplain
natural levees built by repeated floods
the outer edges of an alluvial fan
point bars left by a braided stream
ledges of resistant rock in the walls
quiz.why: When base level falls or discharge increases, the stream cuts down into its alluvium; paired terraces are remnants of the old floodplain.

img.alt: Two block diagrams: at Time 1 a raised base level lets a valley fill with yellow alluvium; at Time 2 a lowered base level lets the stream cut down, leaving terraces on both sides.

quiz.q: Why does Niagara Falls keep moving toward Lake Erie?
options: The dolostone caprock dissolves quickly in the river water
Lake Ontario keeps rising and floods the gorge from below
Shale under the caprock erodes, so the caprock collapses
Winter ice pushes the whole falls upstream each year
Sediment piles up at the base and raises the falls
quiz.why: The dolostone caprock is resistant, but the shale beneath it erodes, so blocks of unsupported dolostone collapse and the falls retreat upstream.

quiz.q: Where is the coarsest sediment on an alluvial fan?
options: At the outer edge of the fan
In the lake beyond the fan
Near the mouth of the canyon
quiz.why: Sediment drops out rapidly where the gradient changes; the coarsest material is near the canyon mouth and gets finer and thinner with distance.

quiz.q: Which description fits a braided stream?
options: One deep channel with tight loops
A dry channel left by stream piracy
A straight, rocky channel in the mountains
A channel cutting through a rising range
Many channels around unstable sand and gravel bars
quiz.why: Braided streams form where channels are choked by sediment; flow splits around bars and occupies many channels.

img.alt: Aerial photo of a wide grey valley floor crossed by many shallow channels splitting and rejoining around gravel bars.

quiz.q: On a meander bend, where does deposition happen?
options: On the cut bank, outside the bend
On the point bar, inside the bend
quiz.why: The fastest water erodes the outside (cut bank); the inside of the bend (point bar) is where sediment is deposited.

img.alt: Four map drawings over time: a gently curving stream erodes on the outside of bends and deposits on the inside, grows point bars, forms a narrow meander neck and finally cuts off, leaving an oxbow lake.

quiz.q: How does an oxbow lake form?
options: A landslide dam blocks a tributary valley
Headward erosion captures a neighbouring stream
Two cut banks meet and a flood cuts through the meander neck
The point bar grows right across the whole channel
Uplift lifts the stream high above its old floodplain
quiz.why: Meander cutoffs occur when cut banks converge and the neck thins; floodwater erodes the neck and the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake.

quiz.q: A mountain range rises across a stream, but the stream keeps cutting straight through it. Why, and what is it called?
options: Uplift is faster than erosion; a diverted stream
It captured another stream; stream piracy
It flows on younger flat layers; a superposed stream
Erosion is faster than uplift; an antecedent stream
Base level rose; a braided stream
quiz.why: If erosion is faster than uplift, the stream cuts through the range: an antecedent stream. If uplift wins, the stream is diverted.

quiz.q: Deltas are sedimentary accumulations at...
quiz.why: A delta forms where a stream enters standing water (its base level). The current slows, loses competence and drops its sediment.

quiz.q: A town lies inside the 100-year flood limit. What is the chance of that flood in any one year?
quiz.why: A 100-year flood has a 1% probability each year. A 2-year flood is 50% and a 500-year flood 0.2%.

img.alt: Block diagram of a valley with a non-flood channel and dashed lines marking the limit of the 2-year flood (50% probability) close to the stream and the 100-year flood (1% probability) farther out.

order.title: From rain to a stream channel
order.prompt: Put the steps in order, from the first at the bottom to the last at the top.
order.why: Water added to the surface first moves as sheetwash down the steepest slope. Sheetwash cuts tiny rills, the rills join, deepen and downcut, and finally the flow is concentrated in one channel that grows uphill by headward erosion.

layers.name: Rain or snowmelt adds water to the surface
Sheetwash moves down the steepest slope
Rills join, deepen and cut down
Flow is concentrated in a single channel

order.title: The life of a meander
order.prompt: Put the stages in order, from the earliest at the bottom to the latest at the top.
order.why: A gentle bend erodes on its outside (cut bank) and builds a point bar inside, so it grows more sinuous. Cut banks converge and the neck thins, a flood cuts through the neck, and the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake that slowly fills with sediment.

layers.name: Cut bank erodes and point bar grows
The neck thins as cut banks converge
A flood cuts through the neck
The loop becomes an oxbow lake
The oxbow lake fills with sediment

order.title: Down the longitudinal profile
order.prompt: Put the places in order going downstream, from the source at the bottom to the mouth at the top.
order.why: A stream starts in steep headwaters, collects tributaries into a trunk stream, meanders across a floodplain on the gentle lower profile and deposits a delta where it meets standing water.

order.title: After base level drops
order.prompt: Put the stages of the landscape in order, from the first at the bottom to the last at the top.
order.why: Uplift lowers base level under swampy, low-relief land. Streams cut in and drain it, then valleys broaden, and finally the land is worn down to a new low-relief landscape at the new base level.

sort.title: Erosion or deposition?
sort.prompt: Sort each feature or change by what mainly makes it.

items.text: Gravel and sand bars of a braided stream

sort.why: Fast water erodes: cut banks, potholes, plunge pools, headward erosion and the downcutting after base level falls. Slowing water deposits: point bars, alluvial fans, deltas, braided bars and the valley fill after base level rises.

sort.title: Which load?
sort.prompt: Sort each description into bed load, suspended load or dissolved load.

items.text: Cobbles that move only at high discharge
Fine particles entrained in the flow
Material that cannot be seen in the water

sort.why: Bed load stays on the bed (rolling, slipping, saltation). Suspended load is fine silt and clay in the flow. Dissolved load is ions from weathering, carried in solution.

sort.title: Permanent or ephemeral?
sort.prompt: Sort each clue by the kind of stream it points to.
sort.why: Permanent streams flow all year where rain and groundwater keep them supplied and little water evaporates. Ephemeral streams dry up where rain is scarce, the water table is low and evaporation is high.
